title: Building technology
summary: Building technology questions are terminology and 'which is used for' pairings, with a small number of code figures. The reliable way through is to hold each item as a purpose: a lintel supports the wall above an opening, a DPC interrupts rising damp, a cavity resists moisture and conducts heat poorly, underpinning deepens a foundation, shoring supports a wall sideways. Learn the temporary-works quartet (shoring, scaffolding, underpinning, timbering) and the bonds carefully — they are examined every sitting.

sections.heading: Foundations
sections.body:
A foundation spreads the structure's load onto ground that can carry it, and takes it below the zone where the ground is unreliable.

**Minimum depth** by Rankine's formula:

> **D = (q/γ) · [(1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ)]²**

In practice, at least **0.5 m below ground**, and always **below** the zone of seasonal moisture change, below any fill, and below the frost line where relevant.

**Types and when each is right** — the discriminator is the *problem being solved*:

| Foundation | Use when |
|---|---|
| **Isolated (spread) footing** | A single column on reasonably good soil |
| **Combined footing** | Two columns too close for separate footings |
| **Strap (cantilever) footing** | A column near a **boundary**, where the footing cannot be centred |
| **Strip / wall footing** | A load-bearing **wall** |
| **Raft (mat)** | **Weak soil and a large loaded area** — footings would otherwise cover more than half the plan |
| **Pile** | The load must reach a **deep** firm stratum, or the soil is very weak throughout |
| **Well / caisson** | Deep water, bridge piers |

Option pairs that are commonly confused: a **raft spreads load** (a shallow foundation), while **piles transfer it downward** (deep). Spreading and transferring are different strategies for different problems, and a raft does nothing to reach a deeper stratum.

A raft's second virtue is that it **ties the structure together**, greatly reducing **differential** settlement — which matters far more than total settlement. A building settling 50 mm uniformly is undamaged; one settling 10 mm unevenly cracks.

**Buoyancy (floating) raft.** Excavating a deep basement removes a weight of soil; if that removed weight approaches the building weight, the **net** pressure increase at foundation level is near zero. A heavy building can then be carried on soil that would not otherwise support it. Such a raft must also be checked for **uplift** where the water table is high.

**Pile types**: by material (timber, concrete, steel), by installation (**driven** or **bored**), and by load transfer (**end bearing** or **friction**). Group spacing is **2.5–3 × diameter**, and **group efficiency is normally less than 1** in clay because the group acts as a block. **Negative skin friction** acts **downward** and must be **subtracted** from capacity — a favourite trap.

sections.heading: Masonry, bonds and walls
sections.body:
The purpose of **bonding** is to **break the continuity of vertical joints** between courses. If vertical joints coincided, the wall would behave as a stack of independent narrow piers instead of one monolith, and a load applied at any point would not distribute sideways.

| Bond | Arrangement | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **English** | Alternate **courses** of headers and stretchers | **Strongest** — a whole header course ties the leaves at once |
| **Flemish** | Headers and stretchers alternating **within every course** | **Better appearance**, more economical in facing bricks, **weaker** |
| **Stretcher** | All stretchers | **Half-brick** walls, partitions, cavity leaves |
| **Header** | All headers | Curved work, one-brick footings |

**English bond for strength, Flemish for appearance** is the trade-off to carry. **Double** Flemish shows the pattern on both faces; **single** Flemish shows Flemish on the face and English behind.

The rules that follow from the purpose: vertical joints must not coincide, the **lap should be ¼ brick**, **queen closers** go **next to the quoin header** (never at the corner itself), brick bats are avoided, and courses must be truly horizontal so the load acts normal to the bed.

**Closers**, examined constantly: a **queen closer** is cut **lengthwise** (half the width); a **king closer** cut **diagonally** across one end; **bevelled** and **mitred** closers are cut at angles.

**Wall thickness** is governed by the **slenderness ratio** — effective height or length ÷ effective thickness — which **IS 1905** limits to about **27** for load-bearing walls. A half-brick wall is far too slender to be load-bearing over a storey height, so it serves only as a partition or a cavity leaf.

**Cavity walls.** Two leaves with a continuous air gap, tied but not bonded. Benefits: **damp resistance** (water crossing the outer leaf runs down the cavity face and drains out) and **thermal insulation** (still air is a poor conductor). Two leaves are **weaker** than one solid wall of the same total thickness, and a cavity wall costs **more** — so strength and economy are never the reason for one.

Construction rules and the reason for each: cavity **50–100 mm**; each leaf at least **100 mm**; **wall ties** at ~900 mm horizontally and 450 mm vertically; ties **sloping down toward the outer leaf** so water runs out; **weep holes** at the base; a **DPC** at the base and stepped over openings; and the cavity kept **clear of mortar droppings**. The last two are where cavity walls actually fail — a **mortar bridge** or a wrongly sloped tie conducts water straight across, and the wall then performs worse than a solid one because the defect is hidden.

**Effective thickness of a cavity wall** (IS 1905 cl. 4.5.3) is the **greater of ⅔(t₁ + t₂) and the thicker leaf** — which formalises the fact that the leaves do not act fully together.

**Mortar must be weaker than the masonry unit.** A weak mortar accommodates movement, so cracks are fine and confined to the joints; a mortar stronger than the brick forces cracking **through the units**, which is far harder to repair.

sections.heading: Damp proofing
sections.body:
**Rising damp** is **capillary action**: water rises through the fine pores of masonry and mortar against gravity, carrying dissolved salts that crystallise on the surface as **efflorescence**. The persistent moisture blisters plaster, peels paint, rots timber and corrodes reinforcement.

Because the water rises through the **material**, the remedy must be a **continuous impervious plane interrupting it** — so **continuity is everything**. A single gap in a DPC defeats the whole barrier.

**Requirements of a DPC:**

> **Impervious** · **continuous over the whole area** · **flexible** enough to accommodate movement · **durable** for the life of the building · not **squeezed out** under the wall load

The last is a real failure mode: too soft a bitumen under a heavy wall extrudes at the face, thinning the layer exactly where it is needed.

**Materials.** The commonest is **bitumen** — hot-applied, as **bituminous felt**, or as a **cement concrete course (about 1:1½:3, 40–75 mm) painted with hot bitumen**, which is standard Nepali and Indian practice. Others: mastic asphalt, metal sheets (lead, copper), bricks of very low absorption, stone slabs, and **integral waterproofing compounds** in the mortar.

Why a plain rigid cement mortar is **not** a DPC on its own: it is brittle, and a DPC sits at a plane where **differential settlement and thermal movement** occur. It cracks, and one crack destroys continuity.

**Where a DPC goes:**

| Location | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **At plinth level**, across the full wall thickness | Stops **rising damp** from the ground |
| Under the floor, as a membrane | Stops damp through the slab |
| Over parapets and copings | Stops water entering from above |
| At sills and lintels | Stops lateral penetration at openings |
| Cavity wall base and over openings | Directs water **out** rather than across |

**Distinguish damp proofing from waterproofing.** Damp proofing resists moisture **without hydrostatic pressure**, as at plinth level. **Waterproofing** resists water **under pressure** — a basement below the water table, a water tank — and needs a far more substantial system.

Measurement, since it is an item-rate matter: **DPC is measured in m², stating the thickness** (IS 1200).

sections.heading: Openings, lintels and arches
sections.body:
An opening creates one problem: the wall above has nothing to stand on. A **lintel** and an **arch** solve it by **opposite mechanisms**.

| | **Lintel** | **Arch** |
|---|---|---|
| Action | **Bending** — flexural | **Compression** only |
| Suits | Materials strong in **tension** — RCC, steel, timber | Materials strong only in **compression** — brick, stone |
| Span | Economical to moderate spans | Larger spans possible |
| Support | Vertical reaction only | Vertical **and horizontal thrust** |
| Construction | Simple; no centering | Needs **centering** until complete |

The **horizontal thrust** is the arch's price: it must be absorbed by a sufficient mass of **abutment**, by a tie, or by an adjacent arch thrusting back. That is why a row of arches needs substantial **end** piers even though the intermediate ones are slender.

**Members of an opening** — all four appear as distractors:

| Member | Position | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Lintel** | Across the **top** | **Supports the wall above** |
| **Sill** | At the **bottom** of a window | Sheds water; finishes the opening |
| **Coping** | On top of a **parapet or wall** | Sheds water off the wall top |
| **Corbel** | Projects from a wall face | **Supports a beam, truss or overhanging member** |
| Jamb | The **vertical sides** | Receives the lintel's load |
| Soffit | The **underside** | — |

**Practical lintel rules.** Bearing at each end is at least **the lintel depth or 100 mm**, whichever is greater. Where the wall above is high, the load on the lintel is **not** the full height of masonry: an **arching action** develops in the brickwork, so only a limited triangular portion is taken as acting on it. A lintel projecting to carry a sunshade is a **chajja**, cast monolithically as a cantilever.

**Arch terminology**: **voussoir** (a wedge-shaped unit), **keystone** (the central voussoir), **springing**, **intrados/soffit**, **extrados**, **haunch**, **crown**, **rise**, **span**. Arch forms: flat, segmental, semicircular, semi-elliptical, pointed, relieving.

**Centering** is the temporary formwork supporting an arch until the mortar has set and the arch can carry itself. Removing it too early is how arches fail during construction.

sections.heading: Floors, roofs and stairs
sections.body:
**Flooring** is chosen by wear, moisture, appearance and cost: **cement concrete** (general), **terrazzo/mosaic** (marble chips in cement, ground and polished), **tiled** (ceramic, vitrified), **granolithic**, **timber**, **brick**, **stone**, **PVC**. Measured in **m²**, deducting the area of walls and columns.

**Roofs.** The timber trusses in **ascending order of span** — the sequence to memorise:

| Truss | Economical span |
|---|---|
| **Lean-to** | up to 2.5 m |
| **Couple / couple close** | up to **4.5 m** |
| **Collar beam** | up to 5 m |
| **King post** | **up to 8 m** |
| **Queen post** | **8 to 12 m** |
| Mansard / truncated | 12 to 18 m |
| **Steel (Fink, Pratt, Howe)** | beyond 12 m |

The progression follows one idea: **as the span grows, more internal members are needed to keep every timber short enough** to avoid excessive bending or buckling.

In a **king post truss**: the **tie beam is in tension** (resisting the outward spread of the rafters), the **principal rafters in compression**, the **struts in compression**, and — the most-missed point — the **king post is in TENSION**. It does not hold the ridge up; it **hangs the tie beam** from the apex so the long tie does not sag. Calling it a post is misleading; it acts as a hanger.

Without a tie, two rafters leaning together would push **outward** at their feet, which masonry cannot resist. The tie converts the arrangement into a **triangle** — the only polygon stiff without rigid joints, and the whole basis of trussing.

Spacing: **timber trusses 3–4 m**, **steel 4–5 m**, with **purlins** spanning between them and **common rafters** on the purlins.

**Stairs.** Empirical comfort rules, R and T in centimetres:

> **R × T = 400 to 450** · **2R + T = 60 to 65** · **R + T = 40 to 45**

They express the same thing three ways: a **large rise demands a small tread**, because the human stride is roughly constant. The **2R + T** form is most used, since a step costs twice as much effort to climb as to traverse.

| Element | Residential | Public |
|---|---|---|
| **Rise** | 15–19 cm | 12–15 cm |
| **Tread** | 25–30 cm | 30–35 cm |
| **Width** | 90 cm minimum | 150–200 cm |
| **Pitch** | up to ~38° | 25–33° |
| Headroom | **2.1 m minimum** | 2.1 m |
| Flight | ≤ **12 steps** before a landing | same |

Public stairs are **shallower and wider** because they serve crowds and must work as an **escape route** under panic.

The rule that causes real accidents: **every step in a flight must have the same rise.** A single odd riser — usually where a level was adjusted on site — is a genuine trip hazard, because a climber's stride becomes automatic after two or three steps.

In a straight flight the **number of treads is one less than the number of risers**, because the top riser lands on the floor above.

sections.heading: Plastering, finishing and formwork
sections.body:
**Plaster coats**, in order of application:

| Order | Name | Purpose | Thickness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1st** | **Rendering coat** | Levels the surface and **keys to the masonry** | **9–12 mm** |
| 2nd | **Floating coat** | Brings the surface to a true plane | 6–9 mm |
| 3rd | **Finishing (setting or skimming) coat** | The smooth final surface | **2–3 mm** |

Note that "setting coat" and "skimming coat" are **synonyms for the finishing coat** — a standard trap, since a candidate who knows only that term will pick it when asked for the *first* coat.

Coats by situation: **one (12 mm)** for ordinary internal brickwork, **two (12 + 3 mm)** for better internal and external work, **three** for superior work and uneven stone masonry.

**Why each coat must be thin and separately cured.** A thick single coat **shrinks and cracks**; a thin coat shrinks less and is restrained by the surface it keys to. Each coat sets and is kept damp before the next is applied.

**Preparation decides whether plaster stays on:** **rake out joints** to ~20 mm on brickwork (a mechanical key), **hack** smooth concrete for the same reason, **clean and wet** the surface, set **screeds** to establish the plane, and **cure 7–10 days**. The wetting step is not a formality — dry brickwork absorbs water so fast that the cement never hydrates at the interface, and the plaster later sounds hollow and falls off in sheets.

Mixes: **1:4 to 1:6** cement–sand, **1:3** lime–sand. A mix richer than about 1:3 **shrinks excessively and crazes** — richer is not better. Plastering is measured in **m²** with **no deduction for openings up to 0.5 m²**.

**Formwork** must be strong enough for the concrete plus construction loads, **rigid** so it does not deflect, **tight** so grout cannot escape, **smooth** and treated with a release agent, and **easily struck without damaging** the concrete. **Steel** is preferred where reuse is repeated (100–2000+ uses against 8–10 for timber).

**Stripping times (IS 456 Table 11)** for OPC:

| Formwork | Minimum |
|---|---|
| **Vertical faces** of walls, columns, beam sides | **16–24 hours** |
| Soffit to **slabs** (props left) | **3 days** |
| Soffit to **beams** (props left) | **7 days** |
| **Props to slabs** — span ≤ 4.5 m / > 4.5 m | **7 / 14 days** |
| **Props to beams and arches** — span ≤ 6 m / > 6 m | **14 / 21 days** |

The organising principle: a **vertical** face carries **no load**, so it comes off within a day; a **soffit** carries the concrete's own weight; **props** must stay longer still because the member must also carry construction loads. So the times rise with the **load carried** and the **span** — never arbitrary numbers.

The distinction between removing the **soffit form** and removing the **props** is where collapses happen: stripping the plywood at 3 days while leaving props standing lets formwork be reused early without asking young concrete to span.

These times must be **extended** in cold weather and with **PPC or mineral admixtures**, and may be **shortened** on the basis of **site-cured cube results** — the professional way to accelerate a programme rather than guessing.

sections.heading: Temporary works — shoring, scaffolding, underpinning, timbering
sections.body:
All four are used around an existing structure, which is why they are so easily confused. The discriminator is simple:

| Term | What it does | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Shoring** | **Temporarily supports** an unsafe, bulging or cracked wall | Against the **side** |
| **Scaffolding** | Provides a **working platform** for labour and material | Alongside the work |
| **Underpinning** | **Strengthens or deepens a foundation** | **Below** the existing foundation |
| **Timbering** | Supports the **sides of an excavation** | In a trench |
| Grouting | Injects cement or chemical to **fill voids or improve soil** | Into the ground |

**Shoring** types: **raking** (inclined props against the wall), **flying/horizontal** (spanning between two walls across a gap), **dead/vertical** (carrying a load from above, as when a wall below is removed).

**Underpinning** is needed when a building is **settling**, when a **basement is added below**, when a **deeper adjacent excavation** is planned, when **loads are increased**, or when the soil has **deteriorated**. The third is the commonest cause of dispute in dense urban building — and the most relevant in Kathmandu, where excavating for a new basement removes the lateral support of the soil beneath a neighbour's footing.

Methods: **pit (traditional)** working in **short alternate lengths of 1.2–1.5 m**; **pile**; **needle and pier**; **jacking/pretest**; **grout injection**. The **safety principle throughout** is that first row: **never remove support from a long continuous length at once.** Work proceeds in short alternate bays, each completed and loaded before the next is opened, so the arch action of the masonry above spans the small gap. Ignoring this is how underpinning brings down the building it was meant to save.

**Scaffolding.** **Single** scaffolding has **one row of standards** with putlogs entering holes left in the **wall**, and is called **bricklayer's** scaffolding — used for **brick** masonry, where putlog holes can be left in the joints and filled afterwards. **Double** scaffolding has **two rows**, is self-supporting, and is called **mason's** scaffolding — used for **stone** masonry, where putlog holes are not practicable because the stones are large, irregular and dressed.

Parts: **standard** (vertical), **ledger** (horizontal, parallel to the wall), **putlog** (horizontal, at right angles), **transom**, **bracing**, **boards**, **guard rail and toe board**.

Other kinds: **steel tubular** (the modern general choice), **cantilever/needle** (where the ground cannot be used), **suspended** (hung from the roof — painting and repointing), **trestle** (internal work up to ~5 m), **patented**.

**Safety is the substance of the topic.** Falls from scaffolding are among the commonest causes of construction death. Requirements: **firm base or sole plates**, adequate **diagonal bracing**, platforms fully boarded with **guard rails and toe boards**, safe **access ladders**, no overloading, and **inspection before each use and after any alteration or bad weather**. A scaffold is a **temporary structure that must nevertheless be designed** — which is precisely why it is so often the one that fails.

formulas.label: Minimum depth of foundation (Rankine)
formulas.note: In practice not less than 0.5 m, and below the zone of seasonal moisture change.

formulas.label: Effective thickness of a cavity wall (IS 1905)
formulas.expression: t_{eff} = greater of ⅔(t₁ + t₂) and the thickness of the thicker leaf
formulas.note: The ⅔ factor formalises that the two leaves are tied but not bonded, so they do not act fully together.

formulas.label: Stair comfort rules (R and T in cm)
formulas.note: Three statements of the same idea: a large rise demands a small tread.

formulas.label: Slenderness ratio of a masonry wall
formulas.expression: λ = effective height (or length) / effective thickness ≤ 27
formulas.note: IS 1905 limit for load-bearing walls in cement mortar. A half-brick wall cannot satisfy it over a storey height.

formulas.label: Treads and risers in a flight
formulas.expression: number of treads = number of risers − 1
formulas.note: The top riser lands on the floor or landing above, which needs no tread.
